title: Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia
articleTitle: Statutory Interpretation, Evidentiary Thresholds, and Activity Characterisation Under Division 355: A Legal and Technical Analysis of Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2021] FCAFC 54
subject: R&D Case Law
pdfSource: Federal Court of Australia judgment, as supplied; no source line in the document
summary: On 30 January 2020, the Tribunal decided to affirm the internal review decision and provided reasons for decision (the Reasons). The Tribunal found that the activities registered as core R&D activities were not "core R&D activities", as defined, because they were not carried out by applying a systematic progression of work based on principles of established science, and because they did not proceed from hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, leading to logical conclusions. Further, the Tribunal found that the activities came within the exception in s 355-25(2)(b) of the ITAA 1997 (set out later in these reasons). For the reasons that follow, in our view, the applicant should be granted leave to amend the amended notice of appeal, but the appeal should be dismissed.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Overview of the Proceeding and Judicial Trajectory

The decision of the Full Court of the Federal Court of Australia in Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2021] FCAFC 54 stands as a foundational authority in the jurisprudence governing the Australian Research and Development Tax Incentive (R&DTI). Handed down on 23 April 2021 by a unanimous bench comprising Logan, Griffiths, and Moshinsky JJ, the judgment dismissed the taxpayer's appeal from the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) decision in Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd and Innovation and Science Australia (Taxation) [2020] AATA 126, which had been decided on 30 January 2020 by Deputy President McCabe and Senior Member Poljak. The litigation reached ultimate finality on 2 September 2021 when the High Court of Australia dismissed the taxpayer's application for special leave to appeal in Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2021] HCASL 1636.

In the broader doctrinal evolution of Division 355 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth) (ITAA 1997), Coal of Queensland functions as the essential judicial counterweight to the earlier Full Federal Court decision in Moreton Resources Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2019] FCAFC 120 (271 FCR 211). Whereas Moreton Resources held (at [151]) that section 355-25(1)(b) is capable of applying, depending on the circumstances, to activities conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site, Coal of Queensland distinguishes Moreton Resources on its facts (at [122]), because the activities in question did not involve applying existing technology to a new site for the purpose of generating new knowledge, and confirms (at [135]) that there is no mutual exclusivity between subsections 355-25(1) and 355-25(2), so that the exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b) may apply even to an activity conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge. The ruling confirms that the Tribunal was entitled to find that geophysical surveys, validation drilling, and routine coal analysis in accordance with Australian Standards—even when undertaken within the commercial context of an ambitious, multi-year mining and beneficiation project—were not "core R&D activities" or "supporting R&D activities" where the outcome could have been determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information and experience, where the evidence (which included no R&D plans or documentation) did not show a systematic progression of work from hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, where the activities were not conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge, and where they came within the exclusion for prospecting, exploring or drilling for minerals.
1.2 Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Registered Claim

The appellant, Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd (COQ), held an Exploration Permit for Coal (EPC1235, issued under the Mineral Resources Act 1989 (Qld)) covering approximately 120 square kilometres in the Bowen Basin area of Queensland, about 40 km north-east of Emerald, referred to commercially as the "Wilton Project" and geologically encompassing part of the Fort Cooper Coal Measures (FCCM). The coal seams within the FCCM were known to be heavily banded and characterised by a high level of ash content, geological features that had historically rendered the deposit commercially unviable to extract and process using conventional mining and coal preparation methodologies.

COQ initiated a three-year project aimed at investigating the physical nature and economic viability of mining the tenement, asserting an overarching objective to develop novel coal mining and beneficiation processes capable of upgrading the high-ash, banded coal into a commercially saleable coking coal product. Pursuant to section 27A of the Industry Research and Development Act 1986 (Cth) (IR&D Act), on 30 April 2013 COQ applied to register four putative "core R&D activities" and one putative "supporting R&D activity" conducted during the 2011–12 income year (the 2012 income year). The four registered core activities were titled "Design of selective mining process" (Activity 1.1), "Design of wash-plant beneficiation process" (Activity 1.2), "Design of ultra-fine processing and briquetting" (Activity 1.3), and "Design of the geochemistry model for environmental waste management" (Activity 1.4), the last of which COQ did not press before the Tribunal; as summarised by the Tribunal, the activities conducted in the 2012 income year that required evaluation comprised, first, an airborne SkyTEM electromagnetic survey and a two-dimensional (2D) seismic survey (using onSEIS technology) across the exploration tenement. Second, they comprised a drilling program to validate the survey results and to provide core samples for analysis. Third, they comprised the washability and handleability testing of those samples by A&B Mylec, whose procedures and results were then reviewed by Sedgman, with final reports delivered in June 2012.

In addition to those four putative core activities, COQ registered one supporting R&D activity described as "background research" (Activity 1.1.1), which it contended was directly related to the registered core R&D activity "Design of selective mining process" (Activity 1.1). Across its registration materials and subsequent tribunal and appellate submissions, COQ contended that these 2011–12 field and analytical works constituted the indispensable initial phase of a three-year experimental program to design a bespoke beneficiation process tailored to the unique mineralogical profile of the FCCM deposit.
1.3 The Regulator's Challenge and Administrative Findings

Australia's R&DTI regime operates under a dual-agency administrative model in which Innovation and Science Australia (ISA)—subsequently styled Industry Innovation and Science Australia (IISA) and assisted administratively by AusIndustry—exercises statutory authority over the registration and eligibility determination of R&D activities, while the Commissioner of Taxation (via the Australian Taxation Office (ATO)) administers expenditure substantiation, "at risk" rules, feedstock adjustments, and tax offset assessments. Following a compliance review of COQ's 2011–12 registration, ISA issued a negative finding, determining that none of the activities registered by COQ were "core R&D activities" within the meaning of section 355-25 of the ITAA 1997 or "supporting R&D activities" within section 355-303. That decision, made by a delegate of the Board (ISA) on 28 May 2015 pursuant to section 27J of the IR&D Act, was confirmed by the Board upon internal review under section 30D of the IR&D Act on 27 January 2017.

Upon COQ's application for merits review, the AAT affirmed ISA's decision in its entirety. The Tribunal concluded that the 2011–12 activities were "generic exploration activities" of the precise kind that any mining company holding an exploration tenement would undertake in the initial exploration stages in order to ascertain the location, quality and size of the coal resources so that it could progress to a point of being able to mine the coal. The AAT found, among other things, that the outcome of the A&B Mylec and Sedgman laboratory work (routine coal analysis in accordance with Australian Standards) was predictable based on experience and current knowledge about the FCCM and could have been determined in advance, that the activities were not conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge, that there were no R&D plans or documentation to demonstrate that the activities were carried out by applying a systematic progression of work based on principles of established science or that they proceeded from the purported hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, leading to logical conclusions, and that the activities in any event came within the statutory exclusion for prospecting, exploring, or drilling for minerals under section 355-25(2)(b).
1.4 Governing Statutory Architecture

The statutory framework governing the dispute is anchored in Division 355 of Part 3-45 of the ITAA 1997, read in conjunction with Part III of the IR&D Act. The legislative object of Division 355, articulated in section 355-5(1), is to encourage industry to conduct research and development activities that might otherwise not be conducted because of an uncertain return from the activities, in cases where the knowledge gained is likely to benefit the wider Australian economy. Section 355-5(2) specifies that this object is to be achieved by providing a tax incentive for industry to conduct, in a scientific way, experimental activities for the purpose of generating new knowledge or information in either a general or applied form (including new knowledge in the form of new or improved materials, products, devices, processes or services).

Under section 355-20 of the ITAA 1997, "R&D activities" are bifurcated into "core R&D activities" and "supporting R&D activities". Section 355-25(1) defines "core R&D activities" via a cumulative two-limbed positive test. Under the first positive limb in section 355-25(1)(a), core R&D activities are experimental activities whose outcome cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information, or experience, but can only be determined by applying a systematic progression of work that: (i) is based on principles of established science; and (ii) proceeds from hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, and leads to logical conclusions. Under the second positive limb in section 355-25(1)(b), the experimental activities must be conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge, including new knowledge in the form of new or improved materials, products, devices, processes, or services.
Even where an activity satisfies both positive limbs of section 355-25(1), section 355-25(2) enumerates eight classes of activities that are statutorily excluded from being core R&D activities.

Complementing the core definition, section 355-30(1) defines "supporting R&D activities" as activities that are directly related to core R&D activities. However, under section 355-30(2), if an activity falls within any of the exclusions in section 355-25(2), or if it produces goods or services (or is directly related to producing goods or services), it can only qualify as a supporting R&D activity if it is undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting core R&D activities. Findings made by ISA/IISA under Division 2 of Part III of the IR&D Act (including findings about a registration under section 27J) bind the Commissioner of Taxation for the purposes of calculating notional deductions under section 355-205 and the resulting R&D tax offset under section 355-100 of the ITAA 1997, though the Commissioner retains independent authority to audit and deny expenditure that fails statutory nexus, overseas activity rules, or substantiation requirements.
1.5 Final Holding of the Full Federal Court

On appeal under section 44 of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 (Cth), COQ contended that the AAT had misconstrued and misapplied sections 355-25(1)(a), 355-25(1)(b), 355-25(2)(b), and 355-30, had impermissibly restricted its inquiry to the activities performed in the 2011–12 income year rather than evaluating the overarching three-year project, had made factual findings for which there was "no evidence" or which were "not open", had ignored relevant evidence and failed to give adequate reasons or make findings on material questions of fact, and (by a further amended notice of appeal, for which the Court granted leave) had failed to consider its submission that the 2012-year activities were supporting R&D activities for core R&D activities in later years, namely the work by Taggart and Virginia Tech.

The Full Court (Logan, Griffiths, and Moshinsky JJ) rejected every ground of appeal and dismissed the proceeding. Their Honours held that there was evidence (from both Dr Vince and Dr Euston) supporting the AAT's finding that the outcome of the A&B Mylec and Sedgman coal sample analyses could have been determined in advance within the meaning of section 355-25(1)(a), observing that the fact that precise data or results cannot be known in advance does not mean that an activity's outcome cannot be known or determined in advance, and that the AAT did not proceed on an assumption that R&D plans or documentation were required, but merely took their absence into account as one factor in concluding that the statutory systematic progression of work was not shown. The Court further held that the AAT applied the correct legal test under section 355-25(1)(b) in determining that the activities were not conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge, as, on the Tribunal's findings, they were conducted for the purpose of reiterating the existing state of knowledge by confirming the status of particular samples and merely built on the body of knowledge already available about the FCCM3. Moreover, the Full Court confirmed that the AAT did not misapply section 355-25(1) by evaluating eligibility primarily by reference to the specific activities registered and carried out in the 2011–12 income year, that the AAT's finding that the registered activities came within the prospecting, exploring, and drilling exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b) was supported by its earlier factual findings and the evidence, and that the AAT did not err in rejecting the alternative supporting R&D activity contentions under section 355-30, because the later Taggart and Virginia Tech work represented a conceptually different approach devised only after the disappointing (yet predictable) A&B Mylec and Sedgman results, such that the 2012-year activities were not shown to be directly related to, or undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting, that work.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
2.1 Conflation of Routine Data Acquisition and Geological Variability with Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (Section 355-25(1)(a) First Limb)

A primary doctrinal failure in COQ's case was its conflation of epistemic or empirical ignorance—not knowing the exact physical properties or subterranean contours of a specific geological formation prior to measurement—with scientific or technological uncertainty, where the outcome of an activity cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information, or experience. Before the Tribunal and the Full Court, COQ argued that because the FCCM coal seams were heavily banded and contained variable ash distributions, the precise washability and liberation characteristics of the coal (and, in particular, the precise data produced by the A&B Mylec and Sedgman testing) could not be known in advance without actual testing, and that the Tribunal had wrongly equated whether an outcome can be "known or determined" with whether it can be predicted.

Both the AAT and the Full Federal Court dismantled this contention. As the Full Court explained at [101], adopting the Board's analogy of a routine cholesterol blood test, section 355-25(1)(a), read in its entirety, does not ask whether a taxpayer knows the exact numerical data points that a standard measuring instrument or analytical assay will return; merely because the precise data or results cannot be known in advance does not mean that the activity is one whose outcome cannot be known or determined in advance. When a geologist commissions a 2D seismic survey, an electromagnetic survey, or a core drilling program, or submits coal cores to a laboratory for proximate analysis and float-sink washability testing under established Australian Standards, a competent professional knows in advance what the activity will achieve: namely, it will yield standard geophysical profiles and coal quality metrics within the known operational parameters of those established methodologies.

Consistently with the expert evidence in the case (Dr Vince observed that coal is laid out in seams and, in the main, presents in predictable layers, and that an appropriately qualified professional would expect the highly banded coal to cause poor yields), the natural variability of a geological resource does not, of itself, establish that an activity's outcome cannot be known or determined in advance. Where an entity applies known analytical or surveying methods to characterise a variable natural resource without testing a novel scientific principle or resolving an uncertainty in the underlying technology itself, the outcome may, as in this case, be determinable in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information and experience.
2.2 Absence of a Valid Hypothesis and Failure to Establish a Systematic Progression of Work (Section 355-25(1)(a) Second Limb)

Even if an uncertainty exists, section 355-25(1)(a) mandates that the outcome can only be determined by applying a "systematic progression of work" that is (i) based on principles of established science, and (ii) proceeds from hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, and leads to logical conclusions. COQ's claim suffered from two fatal defects under this limb: first, the absence of a valid scientific hypothesis; and second, a complete structural disconnect between the purported hypothesis and the activities actually performed.

The statute does not itself define "hypothesis"; however, the Board's expert, Dr Vince, whose evidence the Tribunal relied upon, explained that a scientifically formulated hypothesis statement is the initial building block of the scientific method, must contain a testable component, and should be supported by an R&D plan documented prior to undertaking the activities and expressed in forward-looking terms. In Coal of Queensland, the taxpayer's stated hypothesis was framed at a high level of commercial and aspirational generality—essentially proposing that the high-ash, banded coal of the Wilton Project could be extracted and processed in an economically viable manner through the development of an improved beneficiation methodology. Dr Vince described this hypothesis as "extraordinarily long, imprecise, ill-defined" and characterised it, and the other purported hypothesis statements, as statements of the aims and objectives of the activities rather than scientific hypothesis statements; the Tribunal found that the activities did not marry well with the hypothesis statement, and the Full Court found no error of law in its reasoning.

Furthermore, the AAT specifically observed that, having carefully considered the outcome of the activities, "it is apparent they do not marry well with the hypothesis statement", and the Full Court rejected the challenges to the Tribunal's reasoning in that paragraph. Even if COQ had formulated a genuine metallurgical hypothesis regarding a novel beneficiation mechanism—for example, testing a new reagent regime or a modified cyclone separation physics model for interbanded coal—the activities actually conducted in the 2011–12 income year consisted of airborne electromagnetic surveys, 2D seismic lines, exploration borehole drilling, and standard Australian Standard coal quality testing. As the Tribunal found, those field and laboratory activities were focused on determining the size and quality of the FCCM coal deposit and formally checked the conventional thinking; it was only after the A&B Mylec and Sedgman results that COQ turned its mind to new concepts for improved beneficiation processes, and those later activities fell outside the 2011–12 income year. Dr Vince could identify no R&D plan and described the approach as ad hoc, and the Tribunal found no R&D plans or documentation demonstrating a progression from the purported hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, leading to logical conclusions.
2.3 Evidentiary Fatalities: Lack of Contemporaneous R&D Plans and Technical Documentation

A central pillar of the Full Federal Court's judgment (at paragraphs [110]–[115] of the reasons) is its rejection of the contention that the Tribunal erred in taking into account the absence of R&D plans or documentation. Before the Full Court, COQ argued that the Tribunal had not applied the statutory text but had determined the issue on the basis of an a priori assumption that satisfaction of the statutory criteria depends upon the existence of "R&D plans or documentation", relying on Re DBTL and Innovation Australia (2013) 137 ALD 88 (purpose may be established by oral testimony or contemporaneous documentation) and Commissioner of Taxation v Bogiatto [2020] FCA 1139.

The Full Court rejected this submission, holding that its premise was not made out: the Tribunal did not state that R&D plans or documentation were essential to satisfy section 355-25(1); its reference to their absence was a statement about the state of the evidence in the case, and the absence of R&D plans or documentation was one factor taken into account in concluding that the activities were not carried out by applying a systematic progression of work based on principles of established science. Specifically, the Full Court found no error in the AAT's observation that there were "no R&D plans or documentation to demonstrate the activities were carried out by applying a systematic progression of work based on the principles of established science; or that they proceeded from the purported hypothesis to experiment, observation and evaluation, leading to logical conclusions".

From an evidentiary and tax litigation perspective, this holding carries profound second-order implications for Australian corporate taxpayers. In administrative review proceedings before the Tribunal (and in tax appeals under Part IVC of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth)), the taxpayer bears the legal and evidentiary burden of establishing that the registered activities satisfy every statutory element of Division 355. Consequently, although the Full Court accepted that documentation is not a statutory requirement (so that eligibility may in principle be established by other evidence, such as oral testimony), a tribunal is entitled to weigh the evidence where a scientific method is sought to be retrofitted onto routine commercial or exploration records years after the fact (in this case, the hypothesis relied upon was articulated in Mr Vorias's October 2017 witness statement, and Dr Euston formulated his own project summary/plan of the later Taggart and Virginia Tech work in his December 2017 expert report) through R&D consultant narratives or ex post facto witness statements. If an entity genuinely formulates a hypothesis, designs an experiment to isolate and test variables, observes empirical outcomes, and evaluates whether the hypothesis is supported or falsified, that intellectual and physical progression would ordinarily be expected to generate a contemporaneous paper trail (as noted by the Full Court at [114], the Tribunal in Rix's Creek Pty Ltd; Bloomfield Collieries Pty Ltd and Innovation Australia [2017] AATA 645 at [21] accepted that documentation is not a statutory requirement, but observed that documentary evidence is an expected feature of an activity that is systematic, investigative and experimental), such as experimental protocols, laboratory notebooks, R&D project plans, design-of-experiments matrices, and technical evaluation reports. Where the only contemporaneous documents in existence are standard commercial exploration reports, tenement compliance filings, drilling logs, and standard NATA-accredited coal assay certificates, a court or tribunal may draw the inference that the work was conceived and executed as standard exploration and resource evaluation rather than as a scientific experiment.
2.4 Failure of the "Purpose of Generating New Knowledge" Test (Section 355-25(1)(b))

Under section 355-25(1)(b) of the ITAA 1997, an experimental activity qualifies as a core R&D activity only if it is conducted "for the purpose of generating new knowledge (including new knowledge in the form of new or improved materials, products, devices, processes or services)". The Full Federal Court upheld the AAT's conclusion that COQ's 2011–12 activities failed this purposive threshold.

The Court did not hold that site-specific information can never constitute new knowledge: it noted that in Moreton Resources the Full Court found that section 355-25(1)(b) is capable of applying, depending on the circumstances, to activities conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge with respect to the application of an existing technology at a new site, and it distinguished that case because COQ's activities did not involve applying existing technology to a new site for that purpose. On the Tribunal's findings, the relevant distinction was therefore between acquiring new site-specific factual information using existing methodologies and generating new scientific or technical knowledge. While the 2D seismic survey, SkyTEM survey, drilling, and sample analyses undoubtedly provided COQ with factual data it did not previously possess regarding the depth, faulting, thickness, and ash content of the coal seams within its EPC, that information, as the Tribunal found (consistently with Dr Euston's evidence that the activities were carried out, among other things, to confirm previous knowledge of the FCCM), merely built on the body of knowledge already available about the FCCM, and the activities were conducted for the purpose of reiterating the existing state of knowledge by confirming the status of particular samples. On the Tribunal's findings, the activities were not undertaken for the purpose of generating new or improved processes; the Full Court added that, although the question under section 355-25(1)(b) is one of purpose, the nature of the activity and the novelty and predictability of its results may elucidate whether a substantial purpose of the activity is the generation of new knowledge. The Full Court did not lay down a general requirement that "new knowledge" in section 355-25(1)(b) must represent a step-change or be of wider applicability (that formulation reflects the opinion of the Board's expert, Dr Vince, who looked for a major departure from the current level of understanding); rather, it held that it was open to the Tribunal on the evidence to find that these particular activities were not conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge.
2.5 Triggering the Statutory Exclusion for Prospecting, Exploring, or Drilling and the "Dual Purpose" Trap (Section 355-25(2)(b))
Even if COQ had succeeded in satisfying the positive limbs of section 355-25(1), its claim was fatally intercepted by section 355-25(2)(b) of the ITAA 1997.

COQ sought to evade section 355-25(2)(b) by advancing a purposive argument: it contended that the Tribunal should have assessed purpose by reference to the overall multi-year project, that it was already well known that the FCCM were high-ash, poor quality deposits, that the main purpose of its 2011–12 surveys and drilling was to identify the best locations for test pits (costeans) from which bulk samples could be taken for testing directed to new mining and processing methods, and that there was no evidence that the A&B Mylec and Sedgman work was undertaken for determining the expected variability in quality of the deposit.

The AAT and the Full Federal Court rejected this argument on two distinct analytical levels. First, at the level of factual characterisation, the Tribunal's findings (at [85]–[88] of its reasons), which were consistent with the evidence of Dr Euston and Dr Vince and with Mr O'Malley's evidence that the survey work enabled COQ to identify where the better areas of coal were located, supported its conclusion that the activities were focused on determining the size and quality of the FCCM coal deposit, mapping more precisely the location of the deposits (including their depth and depth of weathering), and determining more precisely the expected variability in quality; the weight to be given to the evidence was a matter for the Tribunal. Second, at the level of statutory construction, Coal of Queensland highlights a critical statutory trap regarding dual or multiple purposes. Under the positive limb in section 355-25(1)(b), tribunal authority (such as PKWK and Innovation and Science Australia [2021] AATA 706) has recognised that the purpose of generating new knowledge does not need to be the sole purpose of an activity and can coexist with commercial objectives. However, as the Full Court held at [135], there is no mutual exclusivity between subsections 355-25(1) and 355-25(2): an activity might be conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge, but if the activity is prospecting, exploring or drilling for minerals and the new knowledge in question concerns the location, size or quality of deposits, the exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b) may apply, notwithstanding that the taxpayer may also harbour a secondary or downstream purpose.
2.6 Collapse of Supporting R&D Activities, Temporal Misalignment, and Contractual/Scope Deficiencies (Section 355-30 & Section 27A IR&D Act)

COQ's litigation strategy also exposed three structural and governance failures concerning project scoping, multi-year registration boundaries, and supporting activities. The first structural failure involved temporal misalignment across income years. COQ argued on appeal that the AAT had erred in law by assessing the eligibility of its activities predominantly by reference to the work performed in the 2011–12 income year, rather than evaluating the three-year project as an integrated whole. The Full Federal Court rejected this contention. Under the IR&D Act, registration under section 27A is for R&D activities conducted during an income year, and section 27J requires consideration of whether all or part of the registered activities conducted in the registration year were core or supporting R&D activities, with evidence of activities outside that year relevant only insofar as it sheds light on the characteristics of the activities conducted in that year. While an overarching project may span multiple years, the specific activities registered as core R&D activities in a given income year must themselves satisfy the definition of core R&D activities, or be supporting R&D activities directly related to core R&D activities (which, under section 27J(1)(c) of the IR&D Act, may include core R&D activities registered in an earlier year or yet to be conducted). A taxpayer cannot register routine exploration and baseline data collection in Year 1 as "core R&D activities" merely because it intends to conduct genuine metallurgical experimentation in Year 2 or Year 33.

The second failure involved the derivative collapse of supporting activities and the operation of the "dominant purpose" test under section 355-303. Because none of the registered core activities pressed for the 2011–12 year satisfied section 355-25, COQ's registered supporting activity ("background research") could not be supported by reference to them; and the Full Court rejected COQ's further contention that the 2012-year activities were supporting R&D activities directly related to, and undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting, core R&D activities in later years (namely the Taggart and Virginia Tech work), because the Tribunal's findings showed that work represented a conceptually different approach devised only after the disappointing (yet predictable) A&B Mylec and Sedgman results. Moreover, COQ did contend in the alternative before the Tribunal that its 2011–12 surveys and drilling were supporting R&D activities supporting the excavation of costeans and later testing; because those activities fell within the section 355-25(2)(b) exploration exclusion, section 355-30(2) imposed the heightened dominant purpose test. The Tribunal found that these steps were taken in the course of exploration within the FCCM and came within the exclusion, and that there was no evidence that digging the costeans satisfied any of the requirements of a core R&D activity (Mr Vorias agreed it was just to get a bulk sample); the Full Court found no error in that approach, so the surveys and drilling were not shown to have been undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting core R&D13.

The third deficiency lay in COQ's contractual and third-party scope arrangements. In executing its 2011–12 work program, COQ relied on third parties, including Groundprobe Geophysics (in connection with the SkyTEM survey), A&B Mylec (coal testing) and Sedgman (review of A&B Mylec's procedures and results). The Tribunal found that the A&B Mylec work was routine coal analysis in accordance with Australian Standards, and that although the use of SkyTEM technology for coal was novel, testing its effectiveness was Groundprobe Geophysics' own research project rather than part of COQ's activities, COQ's use of the survey results merely contributing to the accumulation of knowledge about the extent, location and quality of the coal. The judgment does not analyse the terms of COQ's contracts; however, Dr Vince could not identify a scientifically formulated hypothesis statement or a properly formulated R&D plan linking the A&B Mylec work to the wider activities, so nothing in the third-party work corroborated COQ's claim that an experimental progression of work was being executed on its behalf.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory requirement and legal principle examined in Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2021] FCAFC 54 against the taxpayer's specific legal and evidentiary failures and the governing standard of proof established by the Full Federal Court.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure / Contention in Coal of Queensland
Full Federal Court's Standard of Proof & Governing Doctrinal Rule

cells: Chapeau of s 355-25(1) ITAA 1997: "Experimental activities"
Activities must be experimental in character, as informed by the cumulative statutory criteria in paragraphs (a) and (b).

Contended that the registered activities formed part of an overarching multi-year experimental project; the Full Court addressed Moreton Resources [2019] FCAFC 120 for completeness, noting its finding that s 355-25(1)(b) can apply to new knowledge concerning the application of an existing technology at a new site.

Confirming Moreton Resources is distinguishable because the activities did not involve applying existing technology to a new site for the purpose of generating new knowledge; the Tribunal's findings under s 355-25(1)(a) and (b) were open on the evidence.
s 355-25(1)(a) First Limb: Outcome cannot be known or determined in advance
The outcome of the activity cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information, or experience.

Contended that the precise data produced by the A&B Mylec and Sedgman testing could not be known in advance, that the experts were not agreed otherwise, and that the Tribunal wrongly applied a "predictability" test.

Epistemic vs. Technological Uncertainty: That precise data or results cannot be known in advance (cf. the routine cholesterol blood test analogy at [101]) does not mean the activity's outcome cannot be known or determined in advance. Evidence from both experts supported the finding that the outcome of the routine A&B Mylec and Sedgman analysis could have been determined in advance.
s 355-25(1)(a) Second Limb: Systematic progression of work & Hypothesis

Outcome can only be determined by a systematic progression of work based on principles of established science proceeding from hypothesis to experiment, observation, evaluation, and logical conclusions.

Posited a broad commercial objective (developing an economically viable beneficiation process for high-ash coal) as its hypothesis; failed to link 2011–12 field surveys and drilling to that hypothesis.

Hypothesis Nexus & Methodological Rigour: Relying on the evidence, including Dr Vince's view that the purported hypotheses were statements of aims and objectives without a testable component, the Tribunal found the activities did "not marry well with the hypothesis statement" and that no systematic progression from hypothesis to logical conclusions was shown; the Full Court found no error of law.
Evidentiary Substantiation of s 355-25(1)(a) (Judgment at [110]–[115])
The R&D entity bears the onus of proving through credible evidence that the statutory progression of work actually occurred.

Produced no contemporaneous R&D plans, experimental protocols, or evaluation records; argued on appeal that the Tribunal had proceeded on an a priori assumption that R&D plans or documentation were required.

Contemporaneous Documentation Standard: Documentation is not a statutory requirement, and the Tribunal did not treat it as one; the absence of R&D plans or documentation was properly taken into account as one factor, documentary evidence being an expected feature of systematic, experimental activity (Rix's Creek at [21], noted at [114]).
s 355-25(1)(b) ITAA 1997: Purpose of generating new knowledge
The activity must be conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge (including new or improved materials, products, devices, processes, or services).
Asserted that acquiring new geological, geophysical, and washability data about the Wilton Project tenement constituted generating "new knowledge" for its planned beneficiation process.

Site-Specific Data vs. New Knowledge: On the Tribunal's findings, the activities were conducted to reiterate the existing state of knowledge by confirming the status of particular samples and merely built on the body of knowledge already available about the FCCM. Site-specific knowledge from applying existing technology at a new site can qualify (Moreton), but that was not this case; the nature, novelty and predictability of an activity may elucidate its purpose under s 355-25(1)(b) and s 355-53.
s 355-25(2)(b) ITAA 1997: Prospecting, exploring, or drilling exclusion
Excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for minerals for the purpose of discovering deposits, or determining more precisely their location, size, or quality.

Argued that the Tribunal should have assessed purpose by reference to the overall project, that the FCCM's poor quality was already well known, and that the main purpose of the surveys and drilling was to locate test pits for bulk sampling directed to new mining and beneficiation processes.

Strict Carve-Out & Dual Purpose Rule: The Tribunal's finding that the activities were focused on determining the location, size and quality of the FCCM deposit was supported by its factual findings and the evidence. There is no mutual exclusivity between s 355-25(1) and (2): an activity conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge may still fall within the exclusion where it is exploration or drilling and the new knowledge concerns the location, size or quality of deposits ([135]).
s 355-30(1) & (2) ITAA 1997: Supporting R&D activities & Dominant Purpose
Must be directly related to an eligible core R&D activity; if within a s 355-25(2) exclusion or producing goods/services, must be for the dominant purpose of supporting core R&D3.

Registered "background research" (Activity 1.1.1) as a supporting R&D activity directly related to Activity 1.1; alternatively contended that the surveys and drilling were supporting R&D activities for the costeans, the A&B Mylec and Sedgman work, and the later-year Taggart and Virginia Tech work.

Derivative Collapse: A supporting R&D activity must be directly related to core R&D activities, which may be conducted in a later year (s 27J(1)(c)(iii) IR&D Act); here, the later Taggart and Virginia Tech work was a conceptually different approach, so the 2012 activities were not shown to be directly related to it. Furthermore, excluded exploration activities cannot qualify as supporting R&D unless undertaken for the dominant purpose of supporting core R&D3.
s 27A IR&D Act & s 355-25: Annual Registration & Temporal Scope
Eligibility is registered and assessed in respect of the specific activities conducted in the relevant income year, within their project context.
Contended the AAT erred in law by assessing s 355-25(1) predominantly by reference to the 2011–12 activities rather than the three-year beneficiation project as a whole.

Annual Activity Specificity: The Tribunal is entitled and required to evaluate whether the specific activities registered and performed in the relevant income year satisfy the statutory criteria, rather than evaluating the multi-year project as a whole; evidence of later-year activities remains relevant insofar as it sheds light on the characteristics of the activities conducted in that year.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate the practical application of the legal and evidentiary principles established in Coal of Queensland Pty Ltd v Innovation and Science Australia [2021] FCAFC 54, this section presents two detailed industry case studies. Each scenario models an Australian taxpayer confronting the exact statutory vulnerabilities exposed in the judgment and sets out a step-by-step remedial framework covering project governance, hypothesis formulation, contemporaneous documentation, experimentation tracking, and third-party contract structuring.
4.1 Case Study 1: Mineral Processing, Beneficiation, and Subsurface Sensor Characterisation in the Australian Resources Sector
4.1.1 Scenario and Legal Vulnerability Profile

Pilbara Polymetallic Processing Pty Ltd ("PPP") is an Australian resident corporate taxpayer holding an Exploration Licence and a Retention Lease over a complex, finely disseminated refractory copper-gold-cobalt deposit with high carbonaceous shale and talcose gangue content in Queensland. PPP intends to undertake a two-year program to unlock the commercial viability of the deposit. In Year 1, PPP plans to conduct a high-resolution 3D induced polarisation (IP) geophysical survey and a core drilling campaign across the tenement to map high-talc zones and update its JORC Mineral Resource estimate, submit drill core composites to a commercial metallurgical laboratory for standard QEMSCAN mineralogy and Bond Ball Mill Work Index comminution testing, and trial a novel, dual-collector cryo-temperature froth flotation and hydrometallurgical pressure oxidation (POX) circuit at bench and pilot scale to selectively depress carbonaceous talc without passivating gold-bearing arsenopyrite surfaces.

Under the principles affirmed in Coal of Queensland [2021] FCAFC 54, PPP's proposed claim faces immediate disqualification on three fronts. First, bundling the 3D IP survey and resource definition drilling into the core activity triggers the explicit exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b), as those activities are conducted for the purpose of determining more precisely the location, size, and quality of the mineral deposit. Under the principle stated at [135] of Coal of Queensland, the presence of a JORC resource definition purpose means that the exclusion in section 355-25(2)(b) may apply to the entire bundled activity, even if it is also conducted for the purpose of generating new knowledge. Second, positing that the deposit can be processed in an "economically viable manner" is a commercial objective rather than a falsifiable scientific proposition based on established principles of physical chemistry or mineral processing. Third, standard QEMSCAN and Bond Work Index tests performed in accordance with Australian or international standards yield outcomes determinable in advance under section 355-25(1)(a).
4.1.2 Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Statutory Boundary Segregation

To insulate the claim from section 355-25(2)(b) and temporal misalignment, PPP must restructure its internal project governance and AusIndustry registration architecture prior to commencing physical work. PPP must first establish a formal R&D Governance Charter approved by its Board of Directors that bifurcates the company's capital and operational budgets into two separate cost centres: Cost Centre A (Tenement Exploration & JORC Resource Definition, which is wholly excluded from the R&DTI claim) and Cost Centre B (Experimental Refractory Beneficiation & Surface Chemistry R&D).

Under this bifurcated governance structure, the 3D IP geophysical survey and all multi-purpose exploration or JORC resource definition drilling must be allocated strictly to Cost Centre A and omitted entirely from the R&DTI registration. If a specific, narrow-diameter metallurgical twin-hole is drilled after resource definition is complete solely and exclusively to extract a 500 kg bulk sample of carbonaceous ore required to feed the bench-scale flotation and POX reactor, that specific metallurgical extraction hole must be registered not as a Core R&D activity, but as a Supporting R&D Activity under section 355-30(1) and (2). Because drilling falls within section 355-25(2)(b), PPP must document via a contemporaneous Board resolution, an internal Authority for Expenditure (AFE), and a signed Geologist's Certificate that the sole and dominant purpose of that specific twin-hole is to supply physical feedstock for Core R&D Activity 1, and that the core data will not be used to update JORC tonnage or grade models. Similarly, standard QEMSCAN and Bond Work Index baseline tests conducted on the bulk sample must be segregated from the Core R&D Activity and registered as Supporting R&D Activities under section 355-30(1), on the basis that they provide the baseline characterisation directly required to calibrate the experimental flotation variables rather than being claimed as experimental in their own right.
Step 2: Hypothesis Formulation and Experimental Protocol Architecture

PPP must replace its commercial viability narrative with a rigorous, falsifiable scientific hypothesis grounded in physical chemistry and mineral surface thermodynamics, directly satisfying section 355-25(1)(a)(i) and (ii) and section 355-25(1)(b). Prior to initiating laboratory work, PPP's Chief Metallurgist must author a formal R&D Experimental Plan stating the following falsifiable hypothesis: "Based on DLVO (Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek) electrostatic double-layer theory and adsorption thermodynamics, introducing a modified low-molecular-weight lignosulfonate depressant pulsed with ultrasonic cavitation at  during roughing flotation at  will selectively cleave hydrophobic talc-arsenopyrite slime coatings via differential zeta-potential shift (), thereby achieving  arsenopyrite recovery while reducing magnesium silicate gangue entrainment to  without passivating the mineral surface during subsequent low-temperature () pressure oxidation."

To establish that the outcome cannot be known or determined in advance under section 355-25(1)(a), the R&D Experimental Plan must incorporate a comprehensive literature review and expert technical sign-off demonstrating that, under current metallurgical knowledge and experience, ultrasonic cavitation in the presence of lignosulfonates is known to cause secondary oxidation of sulfide surfaces that inhibits downstream POX leach kinetics, and that no theoretical model or prior empirical data can predict whether cavitation at  will induce surface passivation versus selective slime detachment. Furthermore, to satisfy section 355-25(1)(b), the plan must explicitly define the targeted new knowledge as new applied chemical and metallurgical process knowledge regarding the interaction between acoustic cavitation fields, polymeric depressant adsorption kinetics, and sulfide surface passivation thresholds—knowledge that advances mineral processing science beyond mere site-specific ore assaying.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To address the evidentiary weakness discussed at paragraphs [110]–[115] of Coal of Queensland, PPP must institute a mandatory, real-time documentation protocol across the income year. Before bench testing begins, PPP must generate a version-controlled, timestamped Design of Experiments (DoE) matrix isolating independent variables—specifically ultrasonic frequency from  to , lignosulfonate dosage in , pulp pH, and POX residence temperature—against dependent response variables comprising zeta-potential shift, talc recovery percentage, gold/cobalt leach extraction percentage, and elemental sulfur formation.

Every subsequent test run (for example, Tests R-01 through R-48) must be logged contemporaneously in an electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) with immutable timestamps. Each ELN entry must systematically record the specific sub-hypothesis tested, the exact experimental setup and control baseline, raw empirical observations, a technical evaluation of anomalies and failed runs (such as unexpected frother collapse at ), and the logical conclusion reached after each series explaining how that conclusion dictated parameter modifications for the subsequent iteration.
Step 4: Restructuring Third-Party Contractor, Drilling, and Metallurgical Laboratory Agreements

Because PPP will engage an external metallurgical research facility and a drilling contractor, its commercial agreements must be legally restructured to evidence Division 355 compliance and satisfy the "conducted for" and "at-risk" rules. Instead, the SoW must incorporate PPP's DoE Matrix as a binding technical schedule, stipulating that the laboratory acts strictly under the technical direction and experimental control of PPP's Chief Metallurgist to execute bespoke, non-standard ultrasonic-flotation trials.

Finally, the contract must vest all foreground intellectual property, experimental datasets, and process know-how exclusively in PPP, with fees structured on a time-and-materials basis where PPP bears the full financial and technical risk if the experimental beneficiation process fails to achieve the hypothesised separation thresholds.
4.2 Case Study 2: Complex Industrial Process Automation and Algorithmic Control Systems in Variable Manufacturing Environments
4.2.1 Scenario and Legal Vulnerability Profile

AgriTherm BioSystems Pty Ltd ("AgriTherm") is an Australian industrial engineering and food-processing technology company based in Victoria that operates high-throughput continuous thermal pasteurisation and biological fermentation plants. AgriTherm experiences significant batch yield losses because incoming organic agricultural feedstocks exhibit wide seasonal and intra-day variations in moisture content, microbial load, and viscosity. To address this, AgriTherm initiates a project to install an array of near-infrared (NIR) inline sensors, upgrade its programmable logic controllers (PLCs), and develop a machine-learning (ML) predictive control algorithm to dynamically adjust steam injection valves and agitation speeds in real time during commercial production runs. AgriTherm's initial R&D claim registers the entire plant upgrade and 12 months of continuous commercial trial production as a "Core R&D Activity," contending that because incoming agricultural raw materials are highly variable and complex biological systems behave unpredictably under load, the iterative tuning of PLC parameters and ML weights constitutes an experimental activity under section 355-25(1).

Under Coal of Queensland [2021] FCAFC 54 and related Division 355 authorities, AgriTherm's claim is exposed to three fatal objections. First, by analogy with the reasoning in Coal of Queensland, where the variability of an input can be characterised by routine measurement on the basis of existing knowledge and experience, that variability does not by itself establish that an activity's outcome cannot be known or determined in advance under section 355-25(1)(a), nor does industrial complexity equate to experimental activity. Second, repeated testing cycles, iterative parameter tuning, and algorithm performance optimisation directed toward improving known systems do not, without more, constitute a hypothesis-driven systematic progression of work or generate new scientific knowledge under section 355-25(1)(a) and (b). Third, conducting trials during live commercial production without isolating experimental runs from routine manufacturing triggers the section 355-30(2) "dominant purpose" barrier for activities that produce goods or services (or relate directly to producing goods or services), alongside feedstock adjustment liabilities under Subdivision 355-G2.
4.2.2 Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Segregation of Routine Engineering from Experimental Inquiry

Purchasing and installing commercial off-the-shelf NIR sensors, wiring PLC hardware, writing standard data-ingestion pipelines, and performing routine PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) loop tuning to accommodate variable feedstock moisture must be classified as ineligible routine engineering and excluded from Core R&D registration.

AgriTherm's technical governance committee must instead isolate the exact technological bottleneck where established control theory and sensor physics break down. Specifically, in high-velocity multiphase turbulent flow (), steam micro-bubbles scatter NIR wavelengths (), causing non-linear spectral distortion that prevents existing chemometric deconvolution models from distinguishing between bound intracellular water and free thermal condensate within the 50-millisecond actuation window required to prevent thermal protein denaturation. Resolving this specific physical-mathematical unknown is isolated and registered as Core R&D Activity 13.

To prevent live production runs from failing the dominant purpose test under section 355-30(2) or tainting the core activity with a commercial production purpose, AgriTherm must restrict Core R&D Activity 1 to a dedicated offline bypass test-loop rig, or to scheduled, non-commercial quarantine windows where the processing line is taken offline from commercial orders exclusively to run controlled experimental protocols. Any supporting activities involving the preparation of biological feedstock batches for those quarantine test runs must be authorised under a formal Experimental Plant Quarantine Directive proving that the dominant purpose of the run is executing the experimental protocol rather than fulfilling commercial customer supply. Moreover, where marketable output is incidentally produced during those trials, AgriTherm must establish accounting sub-ledgers tracking the expenditure on raw agricultural inputs and energy to calculate mandatory Feedstock Adjustments under section 355-465 of Subdivision 355-G of the ITAA 1997.
Step 2: Hypothesis Formulation and Variable Isolation in Complex Systems

To address the evidentiary deficiencies identified in the case (the absence of a scientifically formulated hypothesis and of an R&D plan), AgriTherm must establish a formal Scientific Protocol Specification prior to coding or testing. In that specification, AgriTherm formulates the following falsifiable mathematical and physical hypothesis: "Applying a physics-informed neural network (PINN) coupled with a Lorenz-Mie radiative transfer scattering inversion kernel to dual-angle ( and  backscatter) NIR spectral streams will decouple multiphase steam-bubble Mie scattering from O-H stretching absorption bands ( and ) in turbulent non-Newtonian flows (), reducing real-time intracellular moisture prediction root-mean-square error (RMSE) to  within a  inference latency budget."

Rather than feeding random daily agricultural batches into the plant and observing general yield improvements—which risks being characterised as routine measurement rather than experimentation—AgriTherm must construct a controlled experimental design where input variables are precisely pre-calibrated. Specifically, the test rig must hold feedstock viscosity and baseline moisture strictly constant across controlled levels while systematically varying injected steam bubble void fraction ( to ) and flow Reynolds number, measuring whether the Lorenz-Mie PINN inversion algorithm accurately recovers the known ground-truth moisture content compared to a standard Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression baseline.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Automated Experimentation Tracking

To address the evidentiary considerations discussed at paragraphs [110]–[115] of Coal of Queensland, AgriTherm must embed automated, contemporaneous R&D record-keeping directly into its software and engineering workflow. Before writing experimental code, the Lead Control Scientist must archive a dated State-of-the-Art Technical Baseline Memorandum documenting why standard chemometric models (such as Standard Normal Variate transformation and PLS regression) fail under multiphase Mie scattering regimes, supported by academic literature citations and empirical baseline failure benchmarks.

Rather than relying on generic Git commit messages or retrospective management summaries, AgriTherm must configure an automated experiment-tracking platform (such as MLflow or Weights & Biases integrated with Jira and Confluence R&D tickets) that logs every experimental iteration contemporaneously. Each logged experiment must automatically record the specific mathematical hypothesis ID, the exact codebase commit hash and physics-kernel hyperparameters, the controlled physical flow-rig dataset ID, the quantitative evaluation metrics (RMSE percentage, inference latency in milliseconds, and spectral residual variance), and a mandatory post-experiment scientist evaluation note explaining why a given mathematical formulation succeeded or failed and how that logical conclusion drove the next experimental iteration.
Step 4: Restructuring Engineering Consultancy and Software Vendor Contracts

Where AgriTherm engages external data science contractors or automation engineering firms to assist in developing the spectral inversion algorithms or constructing the offline bypass test loop, its contracts must be drafted to prevent characterisation as routine commercial software development or standard capital works. Any external software or engineering vendor must be engaged under two separate Statements of Work: SoW A (Commercial Plant PLC Integration & UI Development, which is excluded from R&D expenditure) and SoW B (Experimental Lorenz-Mie Spectral Inversion & Bypass Rig Testing, which is claimed as eligible R&D expenditure).

Contractor agreements under SoW B must legally obligate external personnel to log daily timesheets disaggregated by specific R&D Hypothesis and Experiment IDs rather than generic "software development" or "commissioning" billing codes, ensuring that notional deductions claimed under section 355-205 of the ITAA 1997 can withstand joint IISA and ATO substantiation reviews. Finally, the contractual terms of SoW B must stipulate that the contractor provides specialised technical labour under AgriTherm's direct scientific supervision to execute experiments defined in AgriTherm's Scientific Protocol Specification, with no warranty of commercial fitness for purpose or guaranteed algorithmic performance, thereby confirming that the expenditure is genuinely "at risk" and incurred on experimental activities whose outcome cannot be determined in advance.
4.3 Summary Matrix of Remedial Governance and Evidentiary Controls

To consolidate the operational lessons from both case studies, the following table contrasts the defective pre-restructuring practices against the required post-Coal of Queensland compliance controls across all four governance dimensions.

headers: Defective Practice Disqualified in Coal of Queensland
Remedial Post-Coal of Queensland Standard (Case Studies 1 & 2)

cells: Project Governance & Activity Boundaries
Bundling preliminary exploration and standard assays (and, by extension, live commercial production) with downstream R&D into an undifferentiated multi-year claim.

Formal Board R&D Charter bifurcating cost centres; excising s 355-25(2)(b) exploration; isolating Core R&D to bespoke test rigs or offline quarantine windows; documenting s 355-30(2) dominant purpose for any supporting sample extraction or trial inputs.
Hypothesis Formulation & Uncertainty
Framing commercial viability or system optimisation goals as hypotheses; treating geological or raw material variability as technological uncertainty.

Formulating pre-experiment, falsifiable causal propositions grounded in physical, chemical, or mathematical principles; proving via literature baselines why current knowledge cannot predict the interaction of isolated variables.
Contemporaneous Documentation & Tracking
Relying on routine exploration reports, standard assay certificates, and ex post facto tax consultant narratives without contemporaneous R&D plans.

Archiving pre-commencement R&D Plans, Design of Experiments (DoE) matrices, immutable Electronic Laboratory Notebooks (ELNs), and automated MLflow/Git logs recording failed iterations, empirical observations, and logical conclusions in real time.
Contractual & Third-Party Structuring
Engaging third parties for routine survey, drilling, and Australian Standard coal testing without a linking R&D plan or scientifically formulated hypothesis.

Segregating Statements of Work (R&D vs. Commercial); incorporating the taxpayer's DoE matrix into contractor scopes; mandating experiment-level timesheets; vesting IP in the taxpayer; allocating financial and technical risk to satisfy the "at-risk" rule.
